rationale: Both warn a son against envying sinners; 24:1 also forbids desiring their company, while 23:17 redirects the heart toward reverence for the Lord.
The evil companions' hearts meditate lies; the twisted heart in 6:14 likewise continually devises evils and produces civic disturbance.
Wisdom builds and establishes a house here; 9:1 personifies Wisdom as building her own house and setting its pillars.
Discernment fills storerooms with good wealth; Wisdom likewise promises substance and storehouses filled with good things to those who love her.
Both explicitly rank wisdom above strength; Ecclesiastes extends the comparison to weapons of war, illuminating this proverb's preference for understanding.
Both connect steering and counsel with deliverance: warfare needs deliberation here, while lack of steering causes a fall in 11:14.
Wisdom is located at the gates of the wise here; the opening proclamation likewise places Wisdom publicly at rulers' gates and city gates.
In the continuing contrast with wise deliberation in 24:7, death meets the uneducated; 9:6 urges leaving foolishness and seeking understanding in order to live.
The fool dies in sins here; 5:23 similarly describes an undisciplined person dying and perishing through folly.
The command to rescue people being led to death accords with Isaiah's demand to rescue the wronged and defend those exposed to injustice.
Both say that the Lord examines human hearts and repays each person according to conduct; professed ignorance cannot conceal responsibility from Him.
The honey eaten here introduces the comparison with wisdom in 24:14; 16:24 similarly makes honeycomb sweetness an image of beneficial words.
Both describe a favorable future in which hope does not depart, here for the person who finds wisdom and there for keeping reverence toward the Lord.
The righteous falls and rises again; Micah likewise refuses an enemy's triumph because the fallen speaker will rise with the Lord's help.
Both condemn rejoicing over another person's downfall; 17:5 states that delight in someone perishing will not go unpunished.
This reason for refusing triumph over a fallen enemy invokes the Lord's displeasure; 17:5 likewise places rejoicing at another's destruction under divine accountability.
Both directly prohibit envy of sinners, directing the reader away from treating evildoers as desirable models.
Both portray the impious person's future through an extinguished light; 24:20 calls it a lamp and also denies enduring offspring.
The paired command to fear God and respect the king is closely reflected in Peter's distinct commands to fear God and honor the king.
The warning about punishment follows obedience to God and king; Peter similarly connects submission to rulers with their punishment of evildoers.
Guarding the received word keeps a son outside destruction here; keeping a command likewise guards one's life in 19:16.
The prohibition of false speech to a king corresponds to the king's approval of righteous lips and upright words in 16:13.
The king's tongue acts as a crushing sword here; 16:14 likewise describes royal wrath as a messenger of death.
The sharpened royal wrath consumes people here; 20:2 compares a king's threat to a lion's wrath and warns that provoking him endangers life.
The speaker disclaims human understanding instead of claiming wisdom for himself; 3:7 warns against considering oneself prudent.
The native text positively says God taught the speaker wisdom; 2:6 likewise identifies the Lord as the giver of wisdom, knowledge, and understanding.

The question about ascending to heaven and descending has a close counterpart in John's statement about the Son of Man; the link concerns ascent and descent, not identification of every figure in Proverbs.
Both join God's fire-tested sayings with His protection of those who rely upon Him; Proverbs describes Him as shielding those who revere Him.
Both prohibit adding to the divine word; Proverbs adds that doing so risks reproof and exposure as false.
The prayer for neither wealth nor poverty but sufficient provision corresponds to contentment with food and coverings in First Timothy.
Both warn that becoming full and prosperous can lead to forgetting or denying God; Proverbs also recognizes poverty's separate temptation to steal.
The offspring who curse their father and withhold blessing from their mother enact the opposite of the command to honor father and mother.
A generation declares itself righteous despite remaining unclean; 20:9 similarly challenges anyone's confident claim to a pure heart and freedom from sins.
Lofty eyes and self-exalting eyelids embody the pride condemned in 16:5, where everyone high of heart is unclean before God.
Both picture oppressors as consuming people: swordlike teeth devour the poor here, while Micah portrays rulers stripping flesh and crushing bones.
Both forbid partiality in judgment; Leviticus explicitly requires judging the neighbor righteously rather than favoring social position.
Calling an impious person righteous is condemned in both passages; 17:15 also condemns the converse injustice of declaring the righteous unjust.
Reprovers receive blessing here, while 28:23 promises greater favor to a person who reproves another's conduct than to a flattering speaker.
The warning against being a false witness to a fellow citizen restates the prohibition of false witness against one's neighbor.
Both reject personal repayment of injury; Romans explicitly forbids repaying evil for evil and reserves vengeance for the Lord.
The comparison of the foolish person to a field and vineyard, developed in 24:31-34, resembles the idle person's thorn-strewn ways in 15:19.
The overgrown and abandoned cultivation pictures the consequences of neglect; 15:19 similarly contrasts the idle person's thorns with the courageous person's usable ways.
The observer reconsiders what he sees and chooses discipline; 22:3 likewise contrasts the resourceful person's instruction through observing punishment with fools who pass by unchanged.
Both repeat the lazy person's sequence of a little sleep, a little dozing, and hands clasped over the chest.
Both personify poverty as arriving and want as a runner, making them the consequences of the preceding indulgence in sleep.
The unfilled leech and the refusal to say enough introduce the list in 30:16; 27:20 likewise uses unfilled Hades and destruction to portray insatiable appetite.
Hades appears among things never filled in both passages; 27:20 applies the same insatiability to human eyes.
Both join dishonoring parents with punishment affecting the eyes: ravens peck them out here, while darkness overtakes the offending person's pupils in 20:9a.
The adulterous woman's claim to have done nothing improper resembles the generation that judges itself righteous despite uncleanness; both expose false self-acquittal.
Both pair a fool enjoying material abundance with a household servant raised to rule, presenting these reversals as unfitting or disruptive.
The small creatures' exceptional wisdom corresponds to the bee's advancement through honoring wisdom despite bodily weakness in 6:8c.
Both commend ants for preparing food in summer, using their practical foresight to teach wisdom beyond physical strength.
The rock badgers make homes in rocks here; the psalm similarly calls rock a refuge for rock rabbits, preserving the respective native animal wording.
The locusts march in order despite having no king; Joel's advancing force likewise keeps individual paths and coordinated ranks. This is an image comparison, not an identification of the force.
The native warning links fighting with dishonor, while 20:3 calls withdrawal from abuse honorable and describes fools as becoming entangled in it.
Dragging out words produces disputes as squeezing nostrils produces blood; 15:1 likewise says painful speech stirs anger, contrasting a yielding answer.
A king receives instruction from his mother here; 1:8 explicitly commands the son not to reject his mother's ordinances.
The mother calls her son to keep God's sayings; 6:20 similarly instructs the son to guard paternal laws and retain maternal ordinances.
The warning against giving wealth to women is sharpened by 29:3's specific warning that maintaining prostitutes destroys wealth; the target is a particular related danger.
The instruction that the powerful avoid wine accords with 20:1's association of wine and drunkenness with lack of discipline, insolence, and loss of wisdom.
Both connect powerful men's drinking with corrupt judgment: forgetting wisdom and failing the weak here, and depriving the righteous of their rights in Isaiah.
The native command is to speak God's word and judge everyone soundly; Leviticus supplies the corresponding requirement of righteous, impartial judgment.
Both call for active just judgment on behalf of vulnerable people: the poor and weak here, and the wronged, orphan, and widow in Isaiah.
The king's heart is beyond human examination here; Jeremiah likewise describes the human heart as deep and difficult to know, while distinguishing the Lord's searching knowledge.
The cleansing of unapproved silver introduces removal of wickedness in 25:5; 17:3 also uses metal testing as an image for evaluating human hearts.
Removing the impious makes the throne prosper in righteousness; 16:12 similarly grounds a throne's establishment in righteousness and royal rejection of evil.
Both warn against taking an exalted place for oneself in an honored gathering, because a public demand to yield one's place brings humiliation.
The preferable invitation to come higher closely resembles the host's invitation in Luke, where voluntary humility leads to honor before others.
The warning against rushing into battle corresponds to the honor of turning away from abuse and avoiding the fool's entanglement in conflict.
Withdrawing rather than showing contempt when a friend reproaches resembles the wise person's loving reception of reproof in 9:8.
The command to guard one's ways with readiness for reconciliation corresponds to Jesus' instructions to seek reconciliation and settle promptly with an adversary.
A spoken word is compared to precious gold and carnelian here; 16:24 similarly uses a desirable material image, sweet honeycomb, to commend good words.
The receptive ear makes a wise word precious; 15:32 likewise says the person who keeps rebukes loves his own life rather than rejecting discipline.
Both praise a faithful messenger's benefit to the sender: refreshment in the harvest-heat comparison here, and rescue of a rash king in 13:17.
A soft tongue has surprising power here; 15:1 explains that a yielding answer turns away wrath rather than intensifying it.
Both explicitly limit honey consumption: 25:16 warns that excess makes one vomit, and 25:27 states that eating much honey is not good.
False testimony is compared to a club, sword, and arrow here; 12:18 likewise describes speech that wounds like a sword.
This native saying connects bodily suffering with pain of heart; 17:22 similarly links sorrow with bodily harm, describing a sorrowful person's drying bones.
Grief harms the heart as moth and worm damage materials; 17:22 describes sorrow drying a person's bones, another image of inward distress harming bodily life.
Romans repeats the instruction to feed a hungry enemy and give a thirsty enemy drink, then carries forward the coals-of-fire explanation.
Romans reproduces the image of heaping fiery coals on an enemy's head through feeding and giving drink; Proverbs additionally states the Lord's good repayment.
Both prefer an inhospitable dwelling to sharing a home with a contentious wife: a roof corner here and desert country in 21:19.
Welcome news refreshes like cold water here; 15:30 likewise gives a good report a bodily effect, making bones full.
The judgment that much honey is not good returns to the earlier warning to eat only a sufficient amount and avoid sickness from excess.
The native proverb compares acting without counsel to an unwalled city; 11:14 similarly contrasts falling without steering with deliverance through much counsel.
Both insist that honoring a fool is inappropriate, first by dew at harvest and rain in summer and then by a stone bound in a sling.
An empty curse lands on no one here; Balaam likewise refuses to presume that he can effectively curse someone whom God does not curse.
The rod for a lawless nation resembles the whips and shoulder punishments prepared for the undisciplined and foolish in 19:29.
Both caution against speaking to folly on its own terms: here the danger is becoming like the fool, while 23:9 anticipates contempt for intelligent words.
The paired commands give different reasons for responding to folly: avoid becoming like the fool, yet expose foolishness when silence would confirm self-conceit.
A foolish messenger brings the sender reproach here, whereas 13:17 credits a faithful messenger with rescuing the king who sends him.
Removing a proverb from a fool's mouth corresponds to withholding intelligent words from a fool's ears; both portray wisdom as mishandled by folly.
The stone bound in a sling represents misplaced honor for a fool, matching the earlier comparison of such honor to dew at harvest and rain in summer.
Peter explicitly calls the dog's return to its vomit a true proverb and applies it to returning to defilement, matching Proverbs' return to one's own sin.
Both distinguish shame that produces sin from shame that brings glory and favor, using the same two-part moral distinction.
The person who thinks himself wise is worse off than a fool; 3:7 directly warns against being prudent in one's own estimation.
Both give the lazy person's excuse that a lion is in the roads; 22:13 expands it with imagined murderers in the squares.
The lazy person turns on the bed like a door on hinges; 6:9-10 likewise rebukes remaining asleep instead of getting up.
Both picture a person hiding a hand in the lap and failing even to bring it to the mouth, presenting inactivity as self-defeating.
The lazy person's estimate of his own superior wisdom exemplifies the self-conceit already judged more hopeless than ordinary folly in 26:12.
Interfering in another's dispute is as hazardous as grabbing a dog's tail; 3:30 likewise warns against provoking needless enmity and the harm it can bring.
Ambushing a friend and excusing it as play violates the earlier prohibition against devising evil toward a trusting friend who lives nearby.
Removing the person who fuels conflict quiets battle here; 22:10 likewise says that expelling a pestilent person sends strife out of the council.
The abusive person feeds battle as wood feeds fire; 15:18 similarly identifies the quick-tempered person as the one who prepares battles.
Soft words strike the inward parts here; 5:3-4 likewise contrasts seductive honey-sweet speech with its later bitterness and cutting harm.
Smooth lips conceal a painful heart here; the next portrait makes the mismatch explicit in an enemy whose agreeing lips conceal inward deceit.
The enemy's outward agreement conceals deceit; the following warning explains why a loud entreaty should not persuade the hearer when inward evils remain.
Refusing to trust an enemy's entreaties without considering the hidden evils accords with the resourceful person's reconsideration instead of believing every word.
Concealed enmity establishes deceit here; 26:24 supplies the closely related portrait of an enemy whose agreeable lips hide a heart devising deceits.
Both describe the digger falling into his own pit; Proverbs explicitly directs the pit against a neighbor and adds the returning stone.
The false tongue is opposed to truth here; 12:22 locates the same moral divide in the Lord's rejection of lying lips and approval of faithful deeds.
Both forbid confident boasting about tomorrow because its events are unknown; James applies that limit to plans for travel, trade, and profit.
Praise should come from another rather than one's own mouth; Paul likewise denies that self-commendation establishes approval and points to the Lord's commendation.
Jealousy is portrayed as bearing with no one; the earlier account of a jealous husband similarly describes wrath that refuses ransom or reconciliation.
Open correction is valued above concealed friendship; 28:23 similarly ranks candid reproof above flattering words in the favor it ultimately wins.
The proverb distrusts an enemy's willing kisses; Judas' kiss to identify Jesus for arrest supplies a concrete instance of affectionate appearance used for betrayal.
Misfortunes tear the life apart despite pleasures that delight the heart; 17:22 likewise describes sorrow's destructive effect on the person's bodily life.
Both emphasize durable friendship in times of need; 27:10 particularly values a nearby friend, while 17:17 calls for friendship at all times.
The son's wisdom makes the speaker's heart rejoice in both passages; 23:16 further connects that shared joy with upright speech.
Both contrast the resourceful person's response to observed danger with fools who continue onward and suffer a penalty.
The abusive wife drives a man from his house like winter dripping; 21:19 similarly regards desert dwelling as preferable to life with a contentious wife.
The person who plants a fig tree eats its fruit; Paul similarly appeals to the vineyard planter's right to eat the fruit of his labor.
Both describe the eye as never filled; Proverbs places human visual desire beside the insatiability of Hades and destruction.
The condemned fixing of an eye recalls the malicious man's eye signals in 6:13-14, where bodily gestures accompany a heart devising evil.
Both compare human evaluation with testing silver and gold; 27:21 names praise as the human test, while 17:3 places the choosing of hearts before the Lord.
Both contrast an upright heart's pursuit of discernment or knowledge with the evil orientation of the uneducated or lawless.
Both say that whipping fails to remove a fool's lack of understanding; 17:10 contrasts this with the intelligent person's responsiveness even to a threat.
Attentive knowledge of the flock's lives accords with the righteous person's compassion for the lives of his animals in 12:10.
Gathering grass and mountain fodder for livestock reflects the same timely provision commended in the ant's preparation of food during summer and harvest.
The native verse offers strong sayings for the life of the son and attendants; 4:20-22 likewise says retained words give life and healing to those who find them.
The impious person's flight when nobody pursues repeats the striking image used in Leviticus for the fear accompanying judgment.
Both contrast those who create disputes with the prudent or patient person who extinguishes them.
The vigorous evildoer's extortion of the poor is judged explicitly in 14:31 as an offense against the poor person's Maker.
Loving the law surrounds people with a wall here; 19:16 similarly makes keeping a command a protection for one's own life.
Those who seek the Lord gain understanding of judgment; 2:5-9 likewise connects finding God's knowledge with understanding righteousness and judgment.
Both explicitly prefer a righteous or truthful poor person to a wealthy liar, ranking integrity above possessions.
The understanding son's keeping of law contrasts with conduct that dishonors a father; 13:1 similarly pairs a resourceful son's obedience with the disobedient son's destruction.
Wealth gained by interest and gains is ultimately gathered for someone merciful to the poor; 13:22 similarly stores the impious person's wealth for the righteous.
Turning away from the law compromises prayer here; Isaiah likewise joins God's refusal of supplication with a demand to cease wrongdoing and practice justice.
The person who leads the upright into an evil way falls into destruction himself; 26:27 similarly makes a trap intended for a neighbor recoil on its maker.
The rich man's inflated estimate of his wisdom is challenged here; First Timothy directly warns the rich against arrogance and misplaced confidence in wealth.
Both contrast the communal benefit brought by righteous people with the public harm caused by the impious: glory versus capture here, prosperity versus a razed city there.
The native text says one who explains reproofs will be loved; 9:8 likewise says that reproving a wise person elicits love. The link does not substitute a confession-and-mercy wording.
Both warn of the hard heart's bad outcome: falling into evils here and failing to encounter good things in 17:20.
The tyrant over a needy nation is a hungry lion and thirsty wolf; Ezekiel likewise portrays exploitative leaders as devouring lions and predatory wolves.
The king who hates injustice is promised life, in contrast to extortion; 15:27 likewise opposes destructive bribe-taking to the safety of rejecting unjust gifts.
Both command discipline of a son and promise that he will adorn the parent's life; 28:17a speaks of love and 29:17 of rest.
Righteous walking brings help while crooked walking entangles; 11:5-6 similarly connects straight righteous paths with rescue and lawlessness with self-entrapment.
Both promise bread to the person who works his own land and criticize pursuing empty leisure instead of productive work.
Selling a man for a morsel of bread resembles Amos' condemnation of selling the righteous for silver and the poor for sandals: human justice is sacrificed for gain.
The grudging person's haste to become rich is set beside Paul's warning that desire for riches leads to temptation, snares, and ruin.
The reprover gains more favor than the flatterer; 9:8 likewise says a wise person responds to reproof with love.
Casting away father or mother while denying sin is condemned here; 19:26 similarly condemns dishonoring a father and thrusting a mother away.
Trust in the Lord offers care in contrast to the insatiable person's rash judgment; 3:5 likewise directs confidence toward God instead of one's own wisdom.
Trusting a rash heart is foolish here; 3:5-7 likewise rejects self-reliance in wisdom and calls for trust in God, reverence, and turning from evil.
Both associate provision for the poor with provision for the giver: freedom from need here, and nourishment for the one sharing bread in 22:9.
The righteous groan under impious dominance here; 29:2 similarly says people groan when the impious rule and rejoice when the righteous are praised.
The stiff-necked person's sudden burning has no healing; 6:15 likewise describes the malicious person's sudden destruction as an incurable crushing.
The groaning under impious rule matches the righteous person's groaning in places dominated by the impious in 28:28.
The father's joy when his son loves wisdom restates 10:1's declaration that a wise son makes a father glad.
A righteous king raises up a country while lawlessness tears it down; 14:34 similarly says righteousness exalts a nation and sins diminish peoples.
A net prepared for a friend entangles the setter's own feet; 26:27 likewise makes the neighbor-directed pit and stone recoil on their maker.
The sinning person encounters a great snare; 5:22 likewise says lawless deeds hunt their doer and one's own sins become binding cords.
The righteous person's ability to judge for the needy corresponds to the royal instruction to judge justly and decide the poor and weak person's case.
Wise people turn away the wrath that destructive people inflame; 15:18 likewise opposes a patient peacemaker to the quick-tempered instigator of battle.
The wise person controls the release of anger instead of pouring it all out; 17:27 similarly commends withholding harsh words and patient understanding.
A king's willingness to hear unjust speech corrupts those under him; 17:4 likewise associates evil with listening to lawless tongues and righteousness with rejecting lies.
The Lord inspects lender and debtor together here; 22:2 similarly brings rich and poor together before the Lord who made both, placing unequal parties under one divine regard.
A throne is established through truthful judgment of the poor here; 16:12 likewise grounds a throne's preparation in righteousness rather than evil.
Blows and reproofs are presented as formative discipline; 13:24 likewise associates careful correction of a son with parental love rather than neglect.
Both tell a parent to discipline a son and promise adornment of the parent's life, with rest here and the son's love in 28:17a.
The blessing attached to keeping the law corresponds to the preservation of life attached to keeping a command in 19:16.
Hasty speech is more hopeless than folly here; 18:13 gives a concrete case, calling an answer delivered before listening foolish and reproachful.
Both identify the angry person as an originator of strife or battle, making uncontrolled anger productive of further wrongdoing.
Insolence brings humiliation while the Lord supports the humble with glory; 3:34 likewise contrasts divine opposition to pride with grace for the humble.
The warning about a hearer who fails to report when an oath is imposed corresponds to Leviticus' rule that a knowledgeable witness who does not declare the matter bears sin.
Fear and shame before people become a trap, whereas trust in the Master saves; 7:1a likewise tells the son to honor the Lord and fear no other apart from Him.
Justice for a person comes from the Lord despite the pursuit of leaders' favor; the native 16:33 likewise says all righteous things are from the Lord.
The righteous reject injustice while the lawless reject a straightening way; 15:9 aligns the Lord with righteousness by calling impious ways an abomination to Him.
Both praise a courageous woman; 31:10 values her above costly stones, while 12:4 portrays her as a crown to her husband.
The husband's confidence and benefit from his wife correspond to Sirach's description of a wife's grace and knowledge delighting and strengthening her husband.
The wife's lifelong good toward her husband corresponds to the courageous wife who gladdens him and enables years completed in peace.
The woman's productive textile work resembles Dorcas' making of tunics and garments, recalled by the widows as concrete evidence of her service.
Providing food for the household and assigning servants their work resembles the prudent steward's responsibility to distribute the household staff's ration at the proper time.
The woman braces her arms for work; 13:4 similarly contrasts idle desire with the courageous person's hands actively engaged in care.
The woman recognizes work's benefit and continues through the night; 14:23 likewise associates attentive labor with abundance and pleasure-seeking inactivity with want.
The hands working a spindle belong to the same practical sphere as Dorcas' garment-making, where skilled handwork becomes useful provision for others.
Her hands are opened to the needy and poor; 19:17 explicitly commends mercy toward the poor as a gift whose repayment the Lord undertakes.
Her household is adequately clothed, relieving her husband's anxiety; First Timothy similarly treats provision for one's own household as a serious obligation.
The husband's distinction among elders forms part of the portrait of the capable wife; 12:4 likewise calls a courageous woman her husband's crown.
The native verse describes attentive, lawful speech and a tongue kept in order; 13:3 likewise connects guarding the mouth with preservation of life.
Her secure household occupations and refusal of idle food correspond to 12:11's contrast between working one's land for bread and pursuing empty things.
The woman's mercy in raising her children belongs with First Timothy's commendation of child-rearing, assistance to the afflicted, and a life attested by good works.
Proverbs ranks understanding and fear of the Lord above pleasing appearance; Peter similarly values the inward character of women who hope in God above outward adornment.
